Demand for Grant of Statehood to Delhi 
DR. KARAN SINGH (NCT of Delhi): Delhi Statehood Bill was 
introduced in Parliament in August last year and the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee has given its recommendations. In the recent State 
30

elections, all the political parties promised Statehood for Delhi. This 
received overwhelming support of the electorate. Today, the multiplicity 
of authorities in Delhi has not only reduced efficiency of the Government, 
but has also led to conflicting policies and procedures, causing confusion 
and harassment to the public. Therefore, the Central Government should 
take immediate steps to fulfil its commitment of passing the Delhi 
Statehood Bill. 
Meanwhile, to satisfy the expectations of the public after the elections, 
pending enactment of the Bill, the Home Ministry should directly approve 
several measures. The Transaction of Business Rules should expressly 
provide for consultation with the Chief Minister in matters relating to law 
and order, police and land, transfers and postings of senior officers. The 
Police force should be placed under the control of the State Government 
except in regard to security and matters where the Central Government 
is concerned. Some of the provisions of the Delhi Statehood Bill in the 
present form amount to superimposition on the autonomy of 
democratically elected government and should be suitably amended to 
remove the difficulties pointed out above.

Need for allocation of more Slots for Tamil in Unicode 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to appeal to the 
Government to prevail upon the Unicode Consortium to allot atleast 320 
slots for Tamil. Unicode is a 16 bit-encoding scheme which contains 
characters of all the major world languages. It is being developed by the 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [4 February, 2004] 
Unicode Consortium, which has the major software developers and 
computer manufacturers as members. The Indian Government is also a 
voting member in the Consortium. Since Tamil has a simple script, all its 
313 characters and the special symbols could have been accommodated 
easily. But unfortunately, in Unicode, Tamil is given 128 slots only. Korean 
language has been given 2,177 slots and Singhalese language has been 
given 400 slots, whereas Tamil has got only 128 slots. This has resulted 
in many disadvantages. The space re quirement for a Tamil text in the 
current Unicode is about 50% more than what is required in the all character 
encoding. The time required to communicate Tamil text is also increased 
by about 50% in the current Unicode. Tamil data will be displayed on a 
computer monitor much slower than English and other languages. 
(THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK) in the Chair] 
This is an avoidable, never ending, recurring expenditure. Current 
Unicode will result in enormous drain of the resources of the Tamil 
community the world over. Many crores of rupees will be wasted every 
day for many years to come. Tamil Nadu Government has already 
damanded increasing the slots. Therefore, I request the Government to 
recommend the All Tamil Block Scheme for Tamil with 320 slots to Unicode 
Consortium.

reasons.

Doordarshan Kendra has become a necessity.

Doordarshan Kendra at Kupwara as early as possible. There is adequate

advised to set up a full-fledged D oordarshan Station at Kupwara

SHRI ARUN JAITLEY: Sir, the speech made by Shri M. Rama Jois, 
Governor of Bihar, on the Republic Day of the year 2004 at Patna, has 
invited criticism, as his speech has been viewed as critical of the 
functioning of the State Government. A portion of the speech commenting 
on the law and order situation in the State has been criticised. Article 
163 of the Constitution, inter alia, provides that there shall be a Council 
of Ministers with the Chief Minist er at the head to aid and advise the 
Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or 
under the Constitution, required to exercise his functions or any of them 
in his discretion. Following the spirit of these provisions, the convention 
has been that the Governor reads from the text of official speeches 
provided to him by the State Government. It has been reported in several 
television channels and a few newspapers that the State Government 
had sent an approved speech to be del ivered by the Governor on the 
Republic Day, but the speech was kept aside by the Governor and he 
made his own speech. This is factually incorrect. As per the information 
made available by the Governor's Secretariat, for the last five years, the 
State Government has not sent any approved speech to be delivered by 
the Governor on the occasion of the Republic Day. On 7th January, 2004, 
the State Cabinet Secretary was requested by the Secretary to the

Governor to send an approved speech to be delivered by the Governor 
on Republic Day before 20th January,  2004. However, the Governor's 
Office waited till the last moment, namely, 25th of January, 2004, but no 
speech, approved by the State Gove rnment, was received. In these 
circumstances, the Governor prepared his own speech and delivered it. 
The Governor of a State is a Constitutional authority. He has to act in 
accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. In case, the prepared 
text of the official speech to be made by him at the Republic Day function 
is not provided to him by the State Government, he is free to prepare his 
own speech. It would not be appropriate for the Union Government to 
question his wisdom or to issue any directions to him. Since he has not 
violated any provision of the Constitution by delivering his own speech, 
in the absence of any official text or speech from the State Government, 
it will not be befitting for the Union Government to interfere in the matter.
